## Recap

\begin{itemize}
\item Recall the simple regression model
\begin{equation}
y = \alpha + \beta x + u
\end{equation}

\item \textbf{The exogeneity assumption}
\begin{equation}
E(u \mid x) = E(ux) = Cov(u,x) = 0
\tag{A2}
\end{equation}
 OLS \underline{by construction} imposes the sample analogue:
\[
\sum_i \hat{u}_i x_i = 0
\]
\textcolor{blue}{Is A2 true? What happens if A2 holds, and what happens if it does not?}
\end{itemize}

## Exogeneity
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{$Cov(u, x) = 0$ is true}
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x$ is said to be \emph{exogenous} (this is an econometrics definition, different to that used by economists);
\item the OLS estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is said to be \textbf{unbiased}\footnote{A related property is \emph{consistency}, which is unbiasedness, but only in ``large'' samples.}; and
\item the effect of $x$ on $y$ (given by the OLS estimate $\hat{\beta}$) is said to be \textbf{causal}.
\end{enumerate}


\end{itemize}

## Endogeneity
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{$Cov(u, x) = 0$ is \textcolor{red}{not} true}
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x$ is said to be \textbf{endogenous} (again, this is an econometrics definition);
\item the OLS estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is said to be \textbf{biased}; and
\item the effect of $x$ on $y$ cannot be said to be \textbf{causal}. Rather, it is just a correlation.
\end{enumerate}

In this lecture we explore three ways in which this can happen.
\begin{itemize}
\item Omitted Variables Bias
\item Measurement Error Bias
\item Simultaneity Bias
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## Omitted Variables Bias (OVB)
\begin{itemize}
    \item Suppose the \textbf{true model}(causal model) is
    \begin{equation}
        y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + e.
    \end{equation}
    $e$ is an unobserved error term that captures everything not contained in
   $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$.
    \item A1/A2 still hold:
    \begin{align}
        E(e) &= 0 \tag{A1} \\
        Cov(e, x_1) &= 0 \tag{A2}\\
        Cov(e, x_2) &= 0 \tag{A4}
    \end{align}

\end{itemize}

## Omitted Variables Bias (OVB)
What are the consequences of estimating the model below when $x_2$ is omitted?
    \begin{equation}
        y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + u.
    \end{equation}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Because $x_2$ is not in the model, $u$ now contains $x_2$:
    \begin{equation}
        u = \beta_2 x_2 + e.
    \end{equation}
    \item We know from earlier analysis that
    \begin{equation}
       E(\hat{\beta}_1)
        = \beta_1 + \frac{Cov(u, x_1)}{Var(x_1)},
    \end{equation}
    from which we can write down the bias:
   $$
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1)
        \equiv E(\hat{\beta}_1) - \beta_1
        = \frac{Cov(u, x_1)}{Var(x_1)}.
    $$
\end{itemize}


## Omitted Variables Bias (OVB)
\begin{itemize}
    \item However, the error term $u$ has changed. Now
    \begin{align}
        \operatorname{Cov}(u, x_1)
        &= \operatorname{Cov}(\beta_2 x_2 + e, x_1) \\ \notag
        &= \beta_2 \operatorname{Cov}(x_2, x_1) + \operatorname{Cov}(e, x_1) \\ \notag
        &= \beta_2 \operatorname{Cov}(x_2, x_1) + 0.
    \end{align}
    The last equality uses A2.
    \item Substituting into (5):
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1)
        \equiv E(\hat{\beta}_1) - \beta_1
        = \beta_2 \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_2, x_1)}{\operatorname{Var}(x_1)}
        = \beta_2 \delta_1,
    \end{equation}
    where $\delta_1$ is the ``slope'' parameter in the population model that relates
    $x_1$ and $x_2$:
    $$
        x_2 = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_1 + \text{error}.
    $$
\end{itemize}


## Omitted Variables Bias (OVB)
\textcolor{blue}{$$
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1)
        \equiv E(\hat{\beta}_1) - \beta_1
        = \beta_2 \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_2, x_1)}{\operatorname{Var}(x_1)}
        = \beta_2 \delta_1,
$$}
If we know \emph{a priori} the signs of $\beta_2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(x_2, x_1)$,
we can "sign the bias":

\begin{itemize}
    \item If both terms have the same sign $(+/+)$ or $(-/-)$, then the OLS
    estimator $\hat{\beta}_1$ is \textbf{biased upwards}:
    \[       \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1) > 0.
    \]
    \item If both terms have opposite signs $(+/-)$ or $(-/+)$, then the OLS
    estimator $\hat{\beta}_1$ is \textbf{biased downwards}:
    \[
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1) < 0.
    \]
\end{itemize}

## OVB Example
\begin{block}{\textbf{How much should tuition fees be?}}
In the early 2000s, the claim was that graduates, on average, earn more than \pounds 400{,}000 more than non-graduates over their lifetime.  
This argument was used by the Government at the time to increase tuition fees to \pounds 3{,}200 per year in 2006.  
After that, fees increased to \pounds 9{,}000 per year following the October 2010 Spending Review (and are now \pounds 9{,}250 per year).
\end{block}

\vspace{0.4cm}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \pounds 400{,}000 is only an average and varies by subject, occupation, and other characteristics.
  \item More generally, what is the return to investment in education (schooling)? 5\% per annum? 10\% per annum?
  
\end{itemize}

## OVB Example: The Returns to Education
\begin{itemize}
    \item Suppose:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $y$ is log of hourly wage (\texttt{lhrpay});
        \item $x_1$ is years of schooling (\texttt{educ});
        \item $x_2$ is unobserved innate ability (\texttt{abil}).
    \end{itemize}
    \item Causal model: $\texttt{lhrpay} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{educ} + \beta_2 \texttt{abil} + e$
    \item Estimated model $\texttt{lhrpay} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{educ} + u$
   \end{itemize} 
Does an OLS regression of $y$ (\texttt{lhrpay}) on $x$ (\texttt{educ}) deliver an unbiased estimate?

## OVB Example: The Returns to Education
\begin{itemize}
\item $\operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_2 \delta_1 $
\item What do we expect?
\begin{itemize}
\item We expect both variables to have a positive impact on average earnings
        $(\beta_1 > 0,\; \beta_2 > 0)$;
        \item We expect $x_1$ and $x_2$ to be positively correlated, as individuals with
        more innate ability tend to choose/acquire more education $(\delta_1 > 0)$.
        \item The estimated effect of an extra year of
    schooling, on average, is too high:
    \[
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_2 \delta_1 > 0.
    \]
\end{itemize}
\item We obtained the following regression results. What can we say about $\beta_1$?
    $$ \hat{\texttt{lhrpay}} = 0.584 + 0.083 \texttt{educ}$$
    \end{itemize}
    
## Measurement Error Bias
Occurs everywhere in microeconometrics (indeed, all empirical economics):

\begin{itemize}
    \item Want the average tax rate but only observe the marginal rate.
    \item An individual mis-recalling their years of education many years later.
    \item Age proxying experience in the classic returns-to-education model.
\end{itemize}

## Measurement Error Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item We start with the following true model:
    \begin{equation}
        y = \alpha + \beta x^{*} + \epsilon.
    \end{equation}
    \item Exogeneity Assumption:
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon, x^{*}) = 0.
        \tag{A2}
    \end{equation}
    We write the "$x$" variable as $x^{*}$ to emphasise it is "measured with error":
    \begin{equation}
        x = x^{*} + e.
    \end{equation}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $x^{*}$ is the true variable in (8), known as a \textbf{latent variable}
        \item $x$ is the variable actually in the data
        \item $e$ is the \textbf{measurement error} (ME)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## Measurement Error Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item The key assumptions about $e$ are:
    \begin{align}
        \operatorname{Cov}(e, x^{*}) &= 0, \tag{A5} \\
        \operatorname{Cov}(e, \varepsilon) &= 0, \tag{A6}
    \end{align}
    and that, on average, individuals report $x^{*}$ correctly:
    \[
        E(e) = 0.
    \]
    \item From (9) and (A5) we get:
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{Var}(x) = \operatorname{Var}(x^{*}) + \operatorname{Var}(e).
    \end{equation}
\end{itemize}


## Measurement Error Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item The estimated model is:
    \begin{equation}
        y = \alpha + \beta x + u.
    \end{equation}
Using (5) again, we know that
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\beta})
        \equiv E(\hat{\beta}) - \beta
        = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(u, x)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.
    \end{equation}
    \item Just as before, we need to work out whether $u$ is correlated with $x$.
    Substituting $x = x^{*} + e$ into the true model (8):
    \begin{equation}
        y = \alpha + \beta (x - e) + \varepsilon
        = \alpha + \beta x + (\varepsilon - \beta e).
    \end{equation}
    \item Comparing with (11), the term in brackets is the regression error:
    \begin{equation}
        u = \varepsilon - \beta e.
    \end{equation}
\end{itemize}


## Measurement Error Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item Evaluating the numerator in the bias expression (13):
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}(u, x)
&= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon - \beta e, x^{*} + e) \\
&= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon, x^{*})
  + \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon, e)
  - \beta \operatorname{Cov}(e, x^{*})
  - \beta \operatorname{Cov}(e, e) \\
&= 0 + 0 - 0 - \beta \operatorname{Var}(e) \\
&= - \beta \operatorname{Var}(e) \lessgtr 0.
\end{align*}
    The three zero covariances come from (A2), (A5), and (A6) respectively.
    $\operatorname{Cov}(u, x)$ can be unambiguously signed, negative if $\beta > 0$
    or positive if $\beta < 0$.
    \item Substituting into (12) and using (10):
    \begin{equation}
        E(\hat{\beta})
        = \beta \left( 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var}(e)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)} \right)
        = \beta \frac{\operatorname{Var}(x^{*})}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}
        \equiv \beta \lambda,
        \qquad 0 < \lambda < 1.
    \end{equation}
 In words, the bias pulls $\hat{\beta}$ towards zero whether or not $\beta > 0$.
    This is known as \textbf{attenuation bias}.
\end{itemize}

## Measurement Error Bias

\begin{itemize}
    \item Why is $\lambda$ a positive fraction?
    \[
        \lambda \equiv
        \frac{\operatorname{Var}(x^{*})}
        {\operatorname{Var}(x^{*}) + \operatorname{Var}(e)}.
    \]
    \item Suppose 20\% of the variation in $x$ is due to measurement error.
    Then $\lambda = 0.8$.
    \item The correlation/covariance between $x$ and $e$ is key:
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname{Cov}(e, x)
        &= \operatorname{Cov}(e, x^{*} + e) \\
        &= \operatorname{Cov}(e, x^{*}) + \operatorname{Cov}(e, e) \\
        &= 0 + \operatorname{Var}(e) > 0.
    \end{align*}
    It is always positive and becomes stronger as the measurement error increases.
\end{itemize}

## Simultaneity Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item This is the idea that $x$ causes $y$ in some economic situations, and at
    the same time $y$ causes $x$. In other words, the two variables are determined
    simultaneously.
    \item The classic example is a market:
    \begin{align}
        y_1 &= \alpha_1 y_2 + k_1 + u_1, \qquad \alpha_1 < 0, \\
        y_2 &= \alpha_2 y_1 + \beta_2 z_2 + k_2 + u_2, \qquad \alpha_2 > 0. 
    \end{align}
    where
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the two equations represent demand and supply respectively;
        \item $y_1$ is \textcolor{blue}{quantity} and $y_2$ is \textcolor{blue}{price};
        \item $y_1$ and $y_2$ are endogenous variables (determined in the model);
        \item $z_2$ is exogenous (determined outside the model). In a market for crops,
        $z_2$ might be rainfall $(\beta_2 < 0)$.
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## Simultaneity Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item There are two endogenous variables, two equations, and two exogeneity
    assumptions.
    \item Because $z_2$ is exogenous:
    \begin{align}
        \operatorname{Cov}(u_1, z_2) &= 0, \tag{A7} \\
        \operatorname{Cov}(u_2, z_2) &= 0. \tag{A8}
    \end{align}
    \item $u_1$ and $u_2$ are the unobserved terms in each equation. We assume
    (for tractability):
    \[
        \operatorname{Cov}(u_1, u_2) = 0.
    \]
\end{itemize}


## Simultaneity Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item The OLS estimator for $\alpha_1$ is:
    \[
        \hat{\alpha}_1
        = \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(y_1, y_2)}
        {\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(y_2)}.
    \]
    whose bias is given by the usual formula:
    \[
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\alpha}_1)
        \equiv E(\hat{\alpha}_1) - \alpha_1
        = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(u_1, y_2)}
        {\operatorname{Var}(y_2)}.
    \]
    \item After a lot of algebra (see the Background Notes),
    \[
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\alpha}_1)
        = \frac{\alpha_2}{1 - \alpha_1 \alpha_2}
        \frac{\operatorname{Var}(u_1)}
        {\operatorname{Var}(y_2)}.
    \]
    \item The supply model is upward-sloping, $\alpha_2 > 0$.
    Typically, $\alpha_1 \alpha_2 < 0$, and so this bias is positive.
    \item Some intuition is on the next slide \ldots
    (Wooldridge’s $z_1$ is our $z_2$.)
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}

\end{figure}


## Simultaneity Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item Because $y_2$ is correlated with $u_1$, the OLS estimator suffers from
    simultaneity bias.
    \item When $\alpha_1 < 0$ and $\alpha_2 > 0$, the bias is positive.
    \item Suppose (a) $y_1$ and $y_2$ are logged,
    (b) $u_1$ explains 80\% of the variation in $y_2$,
    and (c) $\alpha_1 = -1$, $\alpha_2 = 1$. Then
    \[
        \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\alpha}_1)
        = \frac{\alpha_2}{1 - \alpha_1 \alpha_2}
        \frac{\operatorname{Var}(u_1)}{\operatorname{Var}(y_2)}
        = \frac{1}{1 - 1 \cdot (-1)} \cdot 0.8
        = 0.4.
    \]
    Then
    \[
        E(\hat{\alpha}_1)
        = \operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\alpha}_1) + \alpha_1
        = 0.4 - 1
        = -0.6.
    \]
    \item OLS estimates the demand curve as more inelastic than it actually is.
\end{itemize}

## Simultaneity Bias
\begin{itemize}
    \item We need an estimator that exploits the exogenous variation in $z_2$,
    i.e.\ it traces out the demand curve as $z_2$ varies.
    \item (The OLS estimator does not include $z_2$ in its formula!)
    \item In the Background Notes, we show that the estimator
    \[
        \tilde{\alpha}_1
        = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_1, z_2)}
        {\operatorname{Cov}(y_2, z_2)}
    \]
    is unbiased:
    \[
        E(\tilde{\alpha}_1) = \alpha_1.
    \]
    \item This is \textbf{Instrumental Variables}.
    \item This slide is non-examinable.
\end{itemize}


## Outlook

\begin{itemize}
    \item There are four main techniques for dealing with endogeneity
    (discussed above):
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{first differences},
        \item \textbf{difference-in-differences},
        \item \textbf{instrumental variables},
        \item \textbf{regression discontinuity}.
    \end{itemize}
    \item But first, we need to discuss the usefulness of \textbf{multiple regression}
    when modelling dummy variables and categorical variables (Lecture 5).
    \item And finally, we discuss three of the four techniques (not RD).
\end{itemize}
